IIR Filter Design: the Bilinear Transform and Butterworth Filters (L10)

Why this matters in the exam: L10 has never been tested. Sample Test 1 covered only L02–L04, so IIR design is a likely question in the final. Tutorial 9 spends five of its nine questions here: Q2 and Q3 (apply the bilinear map), Q4 (prewarp the specs), Q5 (full Butterworth design to a difference equation) and Q6 (order from the pole radius). Sample Test 1 split 20 marks into questions of 4–7 marks. A full design like T9 Q5 is long enough to be a whole 6–8 mark question on its own, and every step depends on the one before it. One slip early on (no prewarp, wrong , not rounded up) wipes out the rest. Practise until the steps feel routine.

1. The core ideas

1.1 Why design an analogue filter first? (L10 slides 4 and 7)

  • Analogue lowpass design is a solved problem. Butterworth, Chebyshev, elliptic and Bessel prototypes have closed-form , order formulas and pole formulas (L10 slides 8–31).
  • So the strategy on L10 slide 4 is: design an analogue filter, then map it to the digital domain with a formula .
  • The map must keep a stable, causal stable and causal, and it should not alias. The bilinear transform does both. That is why L10 calls it “most important”.

1.2 The bilinear transform (L10 slide 4)

Property What it means for you
The LHP of the -plane maps inside the unit circle, once only A stable always gives a stable . There is no aliasing.
The axis maps onto the unit circle Frequency responses map point to point, but the frequency axis is distorted (warped).
DC gain is kept: .
An analogue zero at infinity becomes a digital zero at (). An th-order all-pole gives the numerator .
  • When to use it: any “convert to ” question (T9 Q2, Q3), and step 5 of every IIR design.
  • Trap: the course always takes in design questions (“Let ”, T9 Q5 and Q7). This is safe: cancels in a design where you prewarp (see 1.4). In a pure “convert this ” question, does not cancel. Use the you are given. T9 Q2 has , so .

1.3 Frequency warping (L10 slides 5–6)

On the unit circle (), the analogue and digital frequencies are related by

  • The whole axis is squeezed into . Near DC the map is close to linear (). Near it is very nonlinear.
  • Key consequence: if the analogue filter has gain at , the digital filter has exactly the same gain at , not at .
  • Prewarping (step 2 of the procedure): convert the digital band edges to analogue edges with . Design the analogue filter to those edges. After the bilinear map the edges land back exactly on and .
  • Trap: writing or (no prewarp). The edges come out in the wrong place, and the passband spec can fail (New Question 6 shows this).

1.4 The course’s 6-step design procedure (L10 slide 7, quoted)

  1. Start with the critical parameters for the digital filter:
  2. Pre-warp the critical frequencies to obtain suitable analog equivalents :
  3. Find an analog filter with suitable frequency response .
  4. Find the transfer function — this step depends on the prototype chosen; e.g. Butterworth: poles known from order and cut-off (derived from and ), Chebyshev and elliptic are more complicated
  5. apply bilinear map to and obtain
  6. Check frequency response against specifications

Why cancels: every analogue frequency (, the pole positions) scales by , and the map uses . The scale factor drops out, so is the same for any . New Question 5(e) checks this numerically.

Cutoff : two valid choices. Once is rounded up there is slack, and you can make one band exact:

Choice Formula Effect Where the course uses it

1.6 Doing step 5 by hand quickly: the factor method

Do not expand and substitute into a cubic. Map each factor separately with ( when ), then multiply every factor by for each order:

Then divide everything by the constant term of the denominator so that . Read off the difference equation. Every hand result in this pack was checked against scipy.signal.bilinear. The method reproduces the T9 Q2 and Q5 official coefficients to 4 decimal places.

1.7 Impulse invariance (low priority)

L10 slide 2 says the analogue-to-digital “transformation methods [were] learned in previous lecture”, and slide 17 mentions impulse invariance. No slide in L09 or L10 covers it, and no tutorial uses it. In short:

  • Sample the analogue impulse response: . With partial fractions this means . Each analogue pole maps to .
  • Stability is kept (). However, the frequency response is a sum of shifted copies of , so it aliases. It is only usable for lowpass and bandpass filters that are well band-limited. This is why slide 17 prefers an that beats the stopband spec when impulse invariance is used.
  • Exam priority: low. At most, expect “state one advantage of the bilinear transform over impulse invariance” (answer: no aliasing).

4. Traps that cost marks

  • No prewarp. Using or in a bilinear design moves the edges. New Question 6 shows the passband then fails by 0.66 dB.
  • Wrong . In this course is the minimum passband gain (), not . Putting into the order formula gives nonsense.
  • Rounding down, or not at all. is always the next integer up, even for 2.06 or 4.02.
  • Mixing Hz and rad/s. for digital; for a purely analogue question (T9 Q6). The prewarped with is in “rad/sample-scaled” units. Do not convert it to Hz.
  • Not saying which band you met exactly. Both choices are correct, but the marker needs to see which formula you used, and differs (0.947 vs 1.098 in Worked Example 2).
  • Forgetting the numerator. An th-order all-pole gives zeros at after the bilinear map.
  • Sign errors in the difference equation. gives . A denominator of becomes .
  • Skipping step 6. The procedure ends with “check against specifications”. It takes two lines with the analogue formula at and .

Question 6 (hard, trap-finder) [4 marks] For the specification in Question 5, a student skips prewarping. They use and directly (), then apply the bilinear transform.

Solution

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

IIR DESIGN BY BILINEAR TRANSFORM (L10)  -- take T = 1 in designs (T cancels)
Map:      s = (2/T)(1 - z^-1)/(1 + z^-1)        s=0 -> z=1,  s=inf -> z=-1
Warping:  Omega = (2/T) tan(w/2)    <->   w = 2 arctan(Omega T / 2)
          w = 2 pi f / Fs   (digital);   Omega = 2 pi f (pure analogue only)
6 STEPS: 1 digital specs wp, ws, dp, ds   2 PREWARP wp, ws -> Wp, Ws
         3 analogue |H(W)|   4 H(s)   5 bilinear -> H(z)   6 CHECK specs
BUTTERWORTH  |H(W)|^2 = 1/(1+(W/Wc)^2N)      Wc = 3-dB point = pole radius
 dp = 10^(-Ap/20) (MIN passband gain)   ds = 10^(-As/20)
 N = log[(10^(As/10)-1)/(10^(Ap/10)-1)] / (2 log(Ws/Wp))     ROUND UP
 Wc (passband exact, slide 17) = Wp / (10^(Ap/10)-1)^(1/2N)
 Wc (stopband exact, T9 Q5)    = Ws / (10^(As/10)-1)^(1/2N)   -> say which!
 LHP poles s_k = Wc exp(j(pi/2 + pi(2k+1)/(2N))), k=0..N-1;  H(s)=Wc^N/prod(s-s_k)
 N=2: s^2+1.4142Wc s+Wc^2      N=3: (s+Wc)(s^2+Wc s+Wc^2)
 N=4: (s^2+0.7654Wc s+Wc^2)(s^2+1.8478Wc s+Wc^2)
 Pair at angle th: s^2 - 2Wc cos(th) s + Wc^2
FACTOR METHOD (K = 2/T):
 s+a      -> [(K+a) + (a-K) z^-1] / (1+z^-1)
 s^2+bs+c -> [(K^2+bK+c) + 2(c-K^2) z^-1 + (K^2-bK+c) z^-2] / (1+z^-1)^2
 numerator Wc^N (1+z^-1)^N ; divide by den constant so a0 = 1
 diff eq: y(n) = -a1 y(n-1) - a2 y(n-2) ... + b0 x(n) + b1 x(n-1) ...
CHECK: gain_dB = -10 log10[1+(W/Wc)^2N] at Wp and Ws (= digital gain at wp, ws)
ORDER FROM POLE RADIUS R: Wc = R; N = log(10^(A/10)-1)/(2 log(W1/Wc)), W1 = 2 pi f
IMPULSE INVARIANCE (low priority): h(n)=T ha(nT), pole p -> e^(pT); aliases
